newsitem.title: UK: U.S jobs data looms for a jittery forex market.
newsitem.headline: U.S jobs data looms for a jittery forex market.

text.p: U.S. employment data has been a major focus for the markets in recent months but Friday's figures have got forex traders more jittery than of late.
This time last year stocks and bonds were pole-axed by a totally unexpected 705,000 leap in February non-farm payrolls and a slide in the unemployment rate to 5.5 from 5.7 percent.

Analysts said the market has been setting itself up for a strong set of data this time around, although last year's strong data was in large part due to a bounce back from a negative number in January.

"Underlying signs are still quite positive and weekly jobless claims, data and employment indices from business surveys have been reasonably buoyant," said Tim Fox, Treasury Economist at Standard Chartered.
"There is no real reason to expect a weak set of figures."

A Reuters consensus market forecast shows a 230,000 rise in non-farm payrolls is anticipated, after 271,000 growth in January, and the overall level of unemployment is seen edging down to 5.3 percent from 5.4 percent.

The hourly earnings rate and average workweek will be a focus, particularly after Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's comments last week which convinced many in the market that he is ready to take a pre-emptive shot at inflation.
"To a certain extent the focus has shifted from the payroll number itself to the average earnings," said Ian Morris, International Economist at HSBC James Capel.
Although a strong figure is to some extent priced in, analysts said current bullishness surrounding the dollar meant that any downturn would be regarded as an opportunity to buy.

A strong set of data would hit stocks and bonds and drag the dollar down. Last year the February figure pared 171 points off Wall Street and bond yields staged their biggest one day surge since Iraq invaded Kuwait in August 1990.
And bond yields have been rising lately, with the key long bond currently at 6.8 percent.

"The overall trend in bond yields over the past couple of weeks has been up and I wouldn't be surprised to see it go above seven percent on the payrolls," HSBC's Morris, who is expecting a non-farms rise nearer 325,000, said.
Expectations of a rise in U.S. rates at the March 25 Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting are gathering pace, but opinion is still very much divided.
Even though economic data may be strong, the rallying dollar -- up 11.5 percent on the mark and 5.2 percent on the yen so far this year -- will help keep the lid on inflation.
With the market bullish and tending to price in strong data, the risk is for weaker than anticipated numbers.
"The shock aspect would be if the figures were extraordinarily weak in which case you would see yields slip back and that would tend to undermine the dollar," Standard's Fox said.
"The irony would be that a rally in bond prices would tend to undermine the dollar because yields would be the focus."
